questions.prompt: What makes DCSync fundamentally harder to detect than file-based NTDS.dit extraction?
options: It requires physical access to the domain controller
It uses the legitimate directory replication protocol as designed -- no malware, no file to find, and no shadow copy to spot
It only works during scheduled replication windows
It permanently disables all domain controller logging
questions.explanation: DCSync asks a real DC for credential data through MS-DRSR, the same protocol DCs legitimately use with each other. There is no malicious file or process to detect -- only an authorized-looking request.

questions.prompt: Which Event ID, filtered for replication extended-right GUIDs, is the core DCSync detection?
questions.explanation: Event ID 4662 records an operation performed on an object. Filtered for the Replicating Directory Changes GUIDs and checked against whether the requesting account is a DC computer account, it is the primary DCSync detection.

questions.prompt: What specifically distinguishes a malicious replication request from a legitimate one in 4662 events?
options: The time of day the request was made
Whether the requesting account is a domain controller computer account -- legitimate replication comes from DCs, not user accounts or workstations
The size of the data returned
Whether the request used TCP or UDP
questions.explanation: Replication between DCs is normal and constant. A replication request from a user account, workstation, or member server rather than a DC computer account is the anomaly that signals DCSync.

questions.prompt: Why can DCSync be executed from any domain-joined machine rather than requiring access to a DC?
options: Because it exploits a vulnerability in domain controllers
Because it issues a standard protocol call that any host can make; what matters is holding an account with the replication extended rights, not where the request originates
Because Windows replicates all credentials to every machine by default
It cannot -- DCSync requires code running on a domain controller
questions.explanation: The attack depends on permissions, not position. An account holding the replication rights can issue DRSGetNCChanges from anywhere in the domain, which is exactly why file-based DC monitoring misses it.
